{{short description|Function that quantifies how near a number is to being rational}}

[[File:Dedekind cut at square root of two.svg|thumb|Rational approximations to the [[square root of 2]].]]

In [[mathematics]], an '''irrationality measure''' of a [[real number]] <math>x</math> is a measure of how closely it can be [[Diophantine approximation|approximated]] by a [[rational number]].

If a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f(t,\lambda) </math>, defined for <math>t,\lambda>0</math>, takes positive real values and is strictly decreasing in both variables, consider the following [[Inequality (mathematics)|inequality]]:

:<math>0<\left|x-\frac pq\right|<f(q,\lambda)</math>

for a given real number <math>x\in\R</math> and rational numbers <math>\frac pq</math> with <math> p\in\mathbb Z, q\in\mathbb Z^+</math>. For <math>x\in\R</math>, define <math>R</math> as the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of all <math>\lambda\in\R^+</math> for which the set <math>\left\{\frac{p}{q}\in\Q : \left\vert x-\frac{p}{q}\right\vert < f(q,\lambda)\right\}</math> is finite. Then <math>\lambda(x)=\inf R</math> is called an irrationality measure of <math>x</math> with regard to <math>f.</math> If the set <math>R</math> is [[Empty set|empty]], <math>x</math> is said to have infinite irrationality measure <math>\lambda(x)=\infty</math>.

By definition, there is a sequence <math>(\varepsilon_n)_{n\in\N}</math> converging to 0 such that for every <math>n</math>, the inequality

<math>0<\left|x-\frac pq\right|<f(q,\lambda(x)+\varepsilon_n)</math>

has at most finitely many solutions <math>\frac pq</math>. By the nondecreasing property of <math>f</math> in the second variable, we deduce that the inequality

:<math>0<\left|x-\frac pq\right|<f(q,\lambda(x)+\varepsilon)</math>

has at most only finitely many solutions <math>\frac pq</math> for ''all'' <math>\varepsilon>0</math>.<ref name=":1">{{cite arXiv |eprint=math/0406300 |first=Jonathan |last=Sondow |title=Irrationality Measures, Irrationality Bases, and a Theorem of Jarnik |year=2004 }}</ref>

== Irrationality exponent ==

The '''irrationality exponent''' or '''Liouville–Roth irrationality measure''' is given by setting <math>f(q ,\mu)=q^{-\mu}</math>,<ref name=":1" /> a definition adapting the one of [[Liouville number]]s — the irrationality exponent <math>\mu(x)</math> is defined for real numbers <math>x</math> to be the [[supremum]] of the set of <math>\mu</math> such that <math>0< \left| x- \frac{p}{q} \right| < \frac{1}{q^\mu} </math> is satisfied by an infinite number of [[Coprime integers|coprime]] integer pairs <math>(p,q)</math> with <math>q>0</math>.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last1=Parshin |first1=A. N. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aWfwCAAAQBAJ |title=Number Theory IV: Transcendental Numbers |last2=Shafarevich |first2=I. R. |date=2013-03-09 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-662-03644-0 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=bugeaud>{{cite book | last=Bugeaud | first=Yann | title=Distribution modulo one and Diophantine approximation | series=Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics | volume=193 | location=Cambridge | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | year=2012 | isbn=978-0-521-11169-0 | zbl=1260.11001 | mr=2953186 | doi=10.1017/CBO9781139017732}}</ref>{{rp|246}}

For any value <math>n<\mu(x)</math>, the [[infinite set]] of all rationals <math>p/q</math> satisfying the above inequality yields good approximations of <math>x</math>. Conversely, if <math>n>\mu(x)</math>, then there are at most finitely many coprime <math>(p,q)</math> with <math>q>0</math> that satisfy the inequality.

For example, whenever a rational approximation <math>\frac pq \approx x</math> with <math>p,q\in\N</math> yields <math>n+1</math> exact decimal digits, then

:<math>\frac{1}{10^n} \ge \left| x- \frac{p}{q} \right| \ge \frac{1}{q^{\mu(x)+\varepsilon}} </math>

for any <math>\varepsilon >0</math>, except for at most a finite number of "lucky"  pairs <math>(p,q)</math>.

A number <math>x\in\mathbb R</math> with irrationality exponent <math>\mu(x)\le 2</math> is called a ''diophantine number'',<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tao |first=Terence |date=2009 |title=245B, Notes 9: The Baire category theorem and its Banach space consequences |url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2009/02/01/245b-notes-9-the-baire-category-theorem-and-its-banach-space-consequences/ |access-date=2024-09-08 |website=What's new |language=en}}</ref> while numbers with <math>\mu(x)=\infty</math> are called [[Liouville number]]s.

===Corollaries===

Rational numbers have irrationality exponent 1, while (as a consequence of [[Dirichlet's approximation theorem]]) every irrational number has irrationality exponent at least 2.

On the other hand, an application of [[Borel-Cantelli lemma]] shows that almost all numbers, including all [[algebraic number|algebraic irrational number]]s, have an irrationality exponent exactly equal to 2.<ref name="bugeaud" />{{rp|246}}

It is <math>\mu(x)=\mu(rx+s)</math> for real numbers <math>x</math> and rational numbers <math>r\neq 0</math> and <math>s</math>. If for some <math>x</math> we have <math>\mu(x)\le\mu</math>, then it follows <math>\mu(x^{1/ 2})\le 2\mu</math>.<ref name=":8" />{{Rp|pages=|page=368}}

For a real number <math>x</math> given by its [[Continued fraction|simple continued fraction expansion]] <math>x = [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...]</math> with convergents <math>p_i/q_i</math> it holds:<ref name=":1" />

:<math>\mu(x)=1+\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln q_{n+1}}{\ln q_n}=2+\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln a_{n+1}}{\ln q_n} . </math>

If we have <math>\limsup_{n\to\infty} \tfrac1{n}{\ln |q_n|} \le \sigma</math> and <math>\lim_{n\to\infty} \tfrac1{n}{\ln |q_n x-p_n|} = - \tau</math> for some [[positive real numbers]] <math>\sigma,\tau</math>, then we can establish an upper bound for the irrationality exponent of <math>x</math> by:<ref name=":10" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Chudnovsky |first=G. V. |chapter=Hermite-padé approximations to exponential functions and elementary estimates of the measure of irrationality of π |date=1982 |editor-last=Chudnovsky |editor-first=David V. |editor2-last=Chudnovsky |editor2-first=Gregory V. |title=The Riemann Problem, Complete Integrability and Arithmetic Applications |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/BFb0093516 |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |volume=925 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=299–322 |doi=10.1007/BFb0093516 |isbn=978-3-540-39152-4}}</ref>

:<math>\mu(x)\le 1 + \frac\sigma\tau</math>

==Irrationality base==

The '''irrationality base''' or '''Sondow irrationality measure''' is obtained by setting <math>f(q,\beta)=\beta^{-q}</math>.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":10">{{cite arXiv |last=Sondow |first=Jonathan |title=An irrationality measure for Liouville numbers and conditional measures for Euler's constant |date=2003-07-23 |eprint=math/0307308 }}</ref> It is a weaker irrationality measure, being able to distinguish how well different Liouville numbers can be approximated, but yielding <math>\beta(x)=1</math> for all other real numbers:

Let <math>x </math> be an irrational number. If there exist real numbers <math> \beta \geq 1 </math> with the property that for any <math> \varepsilon >0 </math>, there is a [[Natural number|positive integer]] <math> q(\varepsilon)</math> such that

: <math> \left|x -\frac{p}{q} \right| > \frac 1 {(\beta+\varepsilon)^q}  </math>

for all integers <math>p,q</math> with <math>q \geq q(\varepsilon)</math> then the least such <math>\beta</math> is called the irrationality base of <math>x</math> and is represented as <math>\beta(x)</math>.

If no such <math>\beta</math> exists, then <math>\beta(x)=\infty</math> and <math>x</math> is called a ''super Liouville number''.

If a real number <math>x</math> is given by its [[Continued fraction|simple continued fraction expansion]] <math>x = [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...]</math> with convergents <math>p_i/q_i</math> then it holds:

:<math>\beta(x)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{ \ln q_{n+1}} {q_n}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln a_{n+1}}{q_n}</math>.<ref name=":1" />

===Examples===

Any real number <math>x</math> with finite irrationality exponent <math>\mu(x)<\infty</math> has irrationality base <math>\beta(x)=1</math>, while any number with irrationality base <math>\beta(x)>1</math> has irrationality exponent <math>\mu(x)=\infty</math> and is a Liouville number.

The number <math>L=[1;2,2^2,2^{2^2},...]</math> has irrationality exponent <math>\mu(L)=\infty</math> and irrationality base <math>\beta(L)=1</math>.

The numbers <math>\tau_a = \sum_{n=0}^\infty{\frac{1}{^{n}a}} = 1+\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{a^a} + \frac{1}{a^{a^a}} + \frac{1}{a^{a^{a^a}}} + ...</math> (<math>{^{n}a}</math> represents [[tetration]], <math>a=2,3,4...</math>) have irrationality base <math>\beta(\tau_a)=a</math>.

The number <math>S=1+\frac{1}{2^1}+\frac{1}{4^{2^1}}+\frac{1}{8^{4^{2^1}}}+\frac{1}{16^{8^{4^{2^1}}}}+\frac{1}{32^{16^{8^{4^{2^1}}}}}+\ldots</math> has irrationality base <math>\beta(S)=\infty</math>, hence it is a ''super Liouville number.''

Although it is not known whether or not <math>e^\pi</math> is a Liouville number,<ref name=":7" />{{Rp|pages=|page=20}} it is known that <math>\beta(e^\pi)=1</math>.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last=Borwein |first=Jonathan M. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=i8dlAQAACAAJ |title=Pi and the AGM: A Study in Analytic Number Theory and Computational Complexity |date=1987 |publisher=Wiley |pages= |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|pages=|page=371}}

==Other irrationality measures==
===Markov constant===
{{Main|Markov constant}}
Setting <math>f(q,M)=(Mq^2)^{-1}</math> gives a stronger irrationality measure: the [[Markov constant]] <math>M(x)</math>. For an irrational number <math>x\in\R\setminus \mathbb Q</math> it is the factor by which [[Dirichlet's approximation theorem]] can be improved for <math>x</math>. Namely if <math>c<M(x)</math> is a positive real number, then the inequality

:<math>0<\left|x-\frac pq\right|<\frac{1}{cq^2}</math>

has infinitely many solutions <math>\frac pq\in\mathbb Q</math>. If <math>c>M(x)</math> there are at most finitely many solutions.

Dirichlet's approximation theorem implies <math>M(x)\ge1</math> and [[Hurwitz's theorem (number theory)|Hurwitz's theorem]] gives <math>M(x)\ge \sqrt5</math> both for irrational <math>x</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hurwitz |first=A. |author-link=Adolf Hurwitz |year=1891 |title=Ueber die angenäherte Darstellung der Irrationalzahlen durch rationale Brüche (On the approximate representation of irrational numbers by rational fractions) |url=https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN235181684_0039 |journal=[[Mathematische Annalen]] |language=de |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=279&ndash;284 |doi=10.1007/BF01206656 |jfm=23.0222.02 |s2cid=119535189|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

This is in fact the best general lower bound since the [[golden ratio]] gives <math>M(\varphi)=\sqrt 5</math>. It is also <math>M(\sqrt2)=2\sqrt 2</math>.

Given <math>x = [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...]</math> by its simple [[continued fraction]] expansion, one may obtain:<ref name="WLV">{{Cite book |last=LeVeque |first=William |title=Fundamentals of Number Theory |publisher=Addison-Wesley Publishing Company, Inc. |year=1977 |isbn=0-201-04287-8 |pages=251–254}}</ref>

:<math>M(x)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}{([a_{n+1}; a_{n+2}, a_{n+3}, ...] + [0; a_{n}, a_{n-1}, ...,a_2,a_1])}.</math>

Bounds for the Markov constant of <math>x = [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...]</math> can also be given by <math>\sqrt{p^2+4}\le M(x) <p+2</math> with <math>p=\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_n</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hancl |first=Jaroslav |date=January 2016 |title=Second basic theorem of Hurwitz |journal=Lithuanian Mathematical Journal |volume=56 |pages=72–76 |doi=10.1007/s10986-016-9305-4 |s2cid=124639896}}</ref> This implies that <math>M(x)=\infty</math> [[if and only if]] [[Restricted partial quotients|<math>(a_k)</math> is not bounded]]. The numbers with finite <math>M(x)</math> are called [[Badly approximable number|badly approximable]]. In particular every [[quadratic irrational number]] <math>x</math> is badly approximable.

Any number with <math>\mu(x)>2</math> or <math>\beta(x)>1</math> has an unbounded simple continued fraction and hence <math>M(x)=\infty</math>. A further consequence is <math>M(e)=\infty</math>.

For rational numbers [[E (mathematical constant)|<math>r</math>]] it may be defined <math>M(r)=0</math>.

===Other results===
The values <math>M(e)=\infty</math> and <math>\mu(e)=2</math> imply that the inequality <math>0<\left|e-\frac pq\right|<\frac{1}{cq^2}</math> has for all <math>c\in\R^+</math> infinitely many solutions <math>\frac pq \in \mathbb Q</math> while the inequality <math>0<\left|e-\frac pq\right|<\frac{1}{q^{2+\varepsilon}}</math> has for all <math>\varepsilon\in\R^+</math> only at most finitely many solutions <math>\frac pq \in \mathbb Q</math>. This gives rise to the question what the best upper bound is. The answer is given by:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Davis |first=C. S. |date=1978 |title=Rational approximations to e |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-australian-mathematical-society/article/rational-approximations-to-e/0A59D34AF70DE5ED9A5F3FB1E3703976 |journal=Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=25 |issue=4 |pages=497–502 |doi=10.1017/S1446788700021480 |issn=1446-8107}}</ref>

:<math>0<\left|e-\frac pq\right|<\frac{c\ln\ln q}{q^2\ln q}</math>

which is satisfied by infinitely many <math>\frac pq \in \mathbb Q</math> for <math>c>\tfrac12</math> but not for <math>c<\tfrac12</math>.

This makes [[E (mathematical constant)|the number <math>e</math>]] alongside the rationals and quadratic irrationals an exception to the fact that for almost all real numbers <math>x\in\R</math> the inequality below has infinitely many solutions <math>\frac pq\in\mathbb Q</math>:<ref name=":8" /> (see [[Khinchin's theorem on Diophantine approximations|Khinchin's theorem]])

:<math>0<\left|x-\frac pq\right|<\frac{1}{q^2\ln q}</math>

==Mahler's generalization==
{{Main|Transcendental number theory#Mahler's_classification}}

[[Kurt Mahler]] extended the concept of an irrationality measure and defined a so-called ''transcendence measure'', drawing on the idea of a Liouville number and [[Partition (mathematics)|partitioning]] the transcendental numbers into three distinct classes.<ref name="bugeaud" />

===Mahler's irrationality measure===

Instead of taking for a given real number <math>x</math> the difference <math>|x-p/q|</math> with <math>p/q \in\mathbb Q</math>, one may instead focus on term <math>|qx-p|=|L(x)|</math> with <math>p,q\in\mathbb Z</math> and <math>L\in\mathbb Z[x]</math> with <math>\deg L = 1</math>. Consider the following inequality:

<math>0<|qx-p|\le\max(|p|,|q|)^{-\omega}</math> with <math>p,q\in\mathbb Z</math> and <math>\omega\in\R^+_0</math>.

Define <math>R</math> as the set of all <math>\omega\in\R^+_0</math> for which infinitely many solutions <math>p,q\in\mathbb Z</math> exist, such that the inequality is satisfied. Then <math>\omega_1(x)=\sup M</math> is Mahler's irrationality measure. It gives <math>\omega_1(p/q)=0</math> for rational numbers, <math>\omega_1(\alpha)=1</math> for algebraic irrational numbers and in general <math>\omega_1(x)=\mu(x)-1</math>, where <math>\mu(x)</math> denotes the irrationality exponent.

===Transcendence measure===
Mahler's irrationality measure can be generalized as follows:<ref name=":5" /><ref name="bugeaud" /> Take <math>P</math> to be a polynomial with <math>\deg P \le n\in\mathbb Z^+</math> and integer coefficients <math>a_i\in\mathbb Z</math>. Then define a [[Height function#Height functions in algebra|height function]] <math>H(P)=\max(|a_0|,|a_1|,...,|a_n|)</math> and consider for [[complex number]]s <math>z</math> the inequality:

<math>0<|P(z)|\le H(P)^{-\omega}</math> with <math>\omega\in\R^+_0</math>.

Set <math>R</math> to be the set of all <math>\omega\in\R^+_0</math> for which infinitely many such polynomials exist, that keep the inequality satisfied. Further define <math>\omega_n(z)= \sup R</math> for all <math>n\in\mathbb Z^+</math> with <math>\omega_1(z)</math> being the above irrationality measure, <math>\omega_2(z) </math> being a ''non-quadraticity measure'', etc.

Then Mahler's transcendence measure is given by:

:<math>\omega(z)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\omega_n(z).</math>

The transcendental numbers can now be divided into the following three classes:

If for all <math>n\in\mathbb Z^+</math> the value of <math>\omega_n (z)</math> is finite and <math>\omega(z)</math> is finite as well, <math>z</math> is called an '''S-number''' (of type <math>\omega(z)</math>).

If for all <math>n\in\mathbb Z^+</math> the value of <math>\omega_n (z)</math> is finite but <math>\omega(z )</math> is infinite, <math>z</math> is called an '''T-number'''.

If there exists a smallest positive integer <math>N</math> such that for all <math>n\ge N</math> the <math>\omega_n(z) </math> are infinite, <math>z</math> is called an '''U-number''' (of degree <math>N</math>).

The number <math>z</math> is algebraic (and called an ''A-number'') if and only if <math>\omega(z)=0</math>.

Almost all numbers are S-numbers. In fact, almost all real numbers give <math>\omega(x)=1</math> while almost all complex numbers give <math>\omega(z)=\tfrac12</math>.<ref name=":9" />{{Rp|pages=|page=86}} The number ''e'' is an S-number with <math>\omega(e)=1</math>. The number ''π'' is either an S- or T-number.<ref name=":9" />{{Rp|pages=|page=86}} The U-numbers are a set of measure 0 but still uncountable.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Burger |first1=Edward B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TRNxKFMuNPkC |title=Making Transcendence Transparent: An Intuitive Approach to Classical Transcendental Number Theory |last2=Tubbs |first2=Robert |date=2004-07-28 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-21444-3 |language=en}}</ref> They contain the Liouville numbers which are exactly the U-numbers of degree one.

===Linear independence measure===
Another generalization of Mahler's irrationality measure gives a linear independence measure.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> For real numbers <math>x_1,...,x_n\in \R</math> consider the inequality

<math>0<|c_1x_1+...+c_nx_n|\le\max(|c_1|,...,|c_n|)^{-\nu}</math> with <math>c_1,...,c_n\in\Z</math> and <math>\nu\in\R^+_0</math>.

Define <math>R</math> as the set of all <math>\nu\in\R^+_0</math> for which infinitely many solutions <math>c_1,...c_n \in\mathbb Z</math> exist, such that the inequality is satisfied. Then <math>\nu(x_1,...,x_n)= \sup R</math> is the linear independence measure.

If the <math>x_1,...,x_n</math> are linearly dependent over <math>\mathbb\Q</math> then <math>\nu(x_1,...,x_n)=0</math>.

If <math>1,x_1,...,x_n</math> are [[Linear independence|linearly independent]] algebraic numbers over <math>\mathbb\Q</math> then <math>\nu(1,x_1,...,x_n)\le n</math>.<ref name=":7">{{cite arXiv |last=Waldschmidt |first=Michel |title=Open Diophantine Problems |date=2004-01-24 |eprint=math/0312440}}</ref>

It is further <math>\nu(1,x)=\omega_1(x)=\mu(x)-1</math>.

==Other generalizations==
===Koksma’s generalization===

[[Jurjen Koksma]] in 1939 proposed another generalization, similar to that of Mahler, based on approximations of complex numbers by algebraic numbers.<ref name="bugeaud" /><ref name=":9">{{Cite book |last=Baker |first=Alan |title=Transcendental number theory |date=1979 |publisher=Cambridge Univ. Pr |isbn=978-0-521-20461-3 |edition=Repr. with additional material |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

For a given complex number <math>z</math> consider algebraic numbers <math>\alpha</math> of degree at most <math>n</math>. Define a height function <math>H(\alpha)=H(P)</math>, where <math>P</math> is the [[characteristic polynomial]] of <math>\alpha</math> and consider the inequality:

<math>0<|z-\alpha|\le H(\alpha)^{-\omega^*-1}</math> with <math>\omega^*\in\R^+_0</math>.

Set <math>R</math> to be the set of all <math>\omega^*\in\R^+_0</math> for which infinitely many such algebraic numbers <math>\alpha</math> exist, that keep the inequality satisfied. Further define <math>\omega_n^*(z)=\sup R</math> for all <math>n\in\mathbb Z^+</math> with <math>\omega_1^*(z)</math> being an irrationality measure, <math>\omega_2^*(z)</math> being a ''non-quadraticity measure'',<ref name=":4" /> etc.

Then Koksma's transcendence measure is given by:

:<math>\omega^*(z)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\omega_n^*(z)</math>.

The complex numbers can now once again be partitioned into four classes  A*, S*, T* and U*. However it turns out that these classes are equivalent to the ones given by Mahler in the sense that they produce exactly the same partition.<ref name=":9" />{{Rp|pages=|page=87}}

=== Simultaneous approximation of real numbers ===
{{Main|Subspace theorem}}

Given a real number <math>x\in \R</math>, an irrationality measure of <math>x</math> quantifies how well it can be approximated by rational numbers <math>\frac pq</math> with denominator <math>q\in\mathbb Z^+</math>. If <math>x=\alpha</math> is taken to be an algebraic number that is also irrational one may obtain that the inequality

:<math>0<\left|\alpha-\frac pq\right|<\frac {1}{q^\mu}</math>

has only at most finitely many solutions <math>\frac pq\in \mathbb Q</math> for <math>\mu>2</math>. This is known as [[Roth's theorem]].

This can be generalized: Given a set of real numbers <math>x_1,...,x_n\in \R</math> one can quantify how well they can be approximated simultaneously by rational numbers <math>\frac{p_1}{q},...,\frac{p_n}{q}</math> with the same denominator <math>q\in\mathbb Z^+</math>. If the <math>x_i=\alpha_i</math> are taken to be algebraic numbers, such that <math>1,\alpha_1,...,\alpha_n</math> are linearly independent over the rational numbers <math>\mathbb Q</math> it follows that the inequalities

:<math>0<\left|\alpha_i-\frac{p_i}{q}\right|<\frac {1}{q^\mu}, \forall i\in\{1,...,n\}</math>

have only at most finitely many solutions <math>\left(\frac{p_1}{q},...,\frac{p_n}{q}\right)\in \mathbb Q^n</math> for <math>\mu> 1 + \frac 1n</math>. This result is due to [[Wolfgang M. Schmidt]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schmidt |first=Wolfgang M. |date=1972 |title=Norm Form Equations |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1970824 |journal=Annals of Mathematics |volume=96 |issue=3 |pages=526–551 |doi=10.2307/1970824 |jstor=1970824 |issn=0003-486X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Schmidt |first=Wolfgang M. |title=Diophantine approximation |date=1996 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-09762-4 |series=Lecture notes in mathematics |location=Berlin; New York}}</ref>
